title: Teacher Workflow No. 03 Your Syllabus Says One Thing, Your Exams Grade Another
author: Doan Winkel
summary: Doan Winkel's How to Teach With AI series presents a roughly two-hour audit that compares what a course syllabus claims with what its assessments actually reward. The workflow gathers every graded file with its point values, uploads them to NotebookLM and asks it to list what a student must do to earn an A, ranked by points. The instructor then verifies that list against the real rubrics, because assignment sheets are aspirational and the rubric is what was graded. A chat tool builds a three-column table of objectives claimed and assessed, claimed but never assessed, and assessed but never claimed. The teacher decides row by row whether to rewrite the objective or change the assessment and can have AI draft a midterm blueprint. A ten-minute and a one-row version are offered for busy instructors.
points: The audit has five steps: gather graded files, have NotebookLM list what earns an A, verify against rubrics, build a claims-versus-evidence table, then decide each row.
NotebookLM answers from the supplied files with citations, and any uncited line should be treated as invented and deleted.
Rubrics override assignment prompts when they disagree, because the rubric reflects what was actually graded.
The most revealing output is the third column, where heavily weighted compliance items such as formatting and page counts never appear in the syllabus.
The instructor, not the machine, makes the call on each row, and student work must be anonymised before any file leaves the computer.
quotes: Which means the midterm will measure whatever you happened to emphasize in class, while your syllabus keeps claiming the course teaches critical thinking.
Open last year’s midterm next to your syllabus objectives. Ask one question of each exam section: which stated objective does this measure, and is that where the points are?
NotebookLM answers from the files you gave it and cites where each claim came from. When a line in its list has no citation, treat that line as invented and delete it.
Assignment sheets are aspirational. The prompt says “analyze the case.” The rubric gives most of the points for laying out the facts and a few for the analysis.
When the sheet and the rubric disagree, the rubric wins. The rubric is what you graded.
The third column is the one that will sting. It fills up with compliance: formatting, page counts, following directions, turning things in on time.
Either the objective was never real and you rewrite it to match what you teach, or the objective matters and the assessment has to change.

If any of those files has graded student samples pasted into it, strip the names, strip the grades sitting next to names, and strip anything about an accommodation before the file leaves your computer.
